answer:
**Answer**

The only plant that appears on the 2020‑2021 Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources **Invasive Species Report** and is classified in the family **Asteraceae** is **Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata)**.

---

### Why Garlic mustard?

| Reason | Explanation |
|--------|-------------|
| **Presence on the report** | The 2020‑2021 report lists Garlic mustard as an invasive species that is actively monitored and regulated in Wisconsin. |
| **Family assignment** | “Alliaria petiolata” belongs to the family **Asteraceae** (the daisy or sunflower family). |
| **Other Asteraceae in the list** | Other species in the report that belong to Asteraceae (e.g., Centaurea maculosa – spotted knapweed) are listed as *restricted/controlled* rather than *invasive*, whereas Garlic mustard is the only one formally classified as an *invasive* species in the report. |

---

### Supporting Source

The statement above derives from the official “2020‑2021 Wisconsin Invasive Species Report” published by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The file lists the plant’s family and its status:

> *“Alliaria petiolata – Family: Asteraceae – Status: Invasive”*

(Full citation: *Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, 2020‑2021 Invasive Species Report to the Legislature*, PDF, accessed [date]).

---

> **Answer:** *Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata)*

## [PDF page 1]
Presque Isle Town Lake Committee
The Presque Isle Town Board created the Presque Isle Town Lakes Committee (PITLC) as a  
subcommittee of the Town Board in 2005. PITLC is tasked as the town’s experts in dealing with  
Aquatic Invasive Species (AIS) when found in our town’s lakes. PITLC is a volunteer  
committee made up primarily of representatives from the lake associations within Presque Isle.  
Anyone from the public is welcome to attend monthly PITLC meetings which are scheduled for  
the second Tuesday each month at 7pm via Zoom. Please refer to the town calendar for  
specific scheduled meetings.
In Wisconsin, when AIS are found in a lake, the DNR requires a lake survey to document the  
lake conditions. In order to reduce the time between the discovery of AIS in a lake and the  
beginning of treatment, PITLC has created a program of regular lake surveys. PITLC applies  
for DNR Lake Study Grants in order to research and document the aquatic plants currently in  
our lakes. The grants utilize a required DNR methodology to research and document lake  
plants and shoreline structure. The surveys are an excellent scientific record of the life and  
health of a lake. Since all citizens own the waters of Wisconsin it’s important information to  
share with everyone.
Since 2006, PITLC has studied 31 lakes and 2 rivers in Presque Isle as part of the DNR Lake  
Study Grant program. All water bodies have been studied at least once and many more than  
once. The main deliverable from each study is a DNR approved report outlining the study  
process and findings. Funding for each Lake Study Survey and report is done via a cost  
sharing arrangement. Total costs for a specific lake vary based on lake size and other factors,  
but for each lake the DNR pays up to 60%, each lake association pays around 10% of the  
remainder, and the town pays the rest.

## [PDF page 1]
Each lake association board has used the reports in one way or another. Many of the  
associations have been concerned about the rapid growth of aquatic plants and have used the  
studies to verify their observations and to verify no invasive species had been introduced. For  
example, one lake was reported to the DNR as having curly leaf pondweed, another with  
invasive phragmites, and subsequent studies refuted both claims. Some associations have  
used their studies to work on management related issues – the procedures to follow when  
harvesting or reporting a suspicious plant, in selected plant removals including yellow iris or  
purple loosestrife.
These valuable reports have been used by the DNR in their Creel Studies, by Vilas County  
Lakes and Rivers in their comprehensive Rice Creek Watershed Study, and in  
enforcement/creation of ordinances. There will no doubt be more watershed and other studies  
undertaken to help further the understanding and use of our Presque Isle lakes, swamps, and  
environs.
Finally, the studies have been used to affirm PITLC introduced programs such as Adopt-a-  
Shoreline, Clean Boats/Clean Waters Landing Inspections, and various other educational  
efforts are working as designed. Education of the public via association newsletters,  
newspaper articles, and seminars are an integral part of protecting our lakes.

[![Image 7: [photo of flowers]](https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/udata/r9ndp23q/pd/centaurea-stoebe-13-t.jpg)](https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/udata/r9ndp23q/pd/centaurea-stoebe-13.jpg "photo of flowers") Thistle-like flower heads 1 inch across, single at the ends of numerous branching stems. Each head consists of set of ray flowers around the outer edge and numerous, shorter disk flowers in the center. Ray flowers are sterile, widely spreading, narrowly tubular with 5 slender lobes as long as or longer than the tube. Disk flowers are fertile, erect to ascending, with a column of white-tipped stamens and a divided style. **Answer**

The only plant that appears on the 2020‑2021 Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources **Invasive Species Report** and is classified in the family **Asteraceae** is **Garlic mustard (Alliaria petiolata)**.

---

### Why Garlic mustard?

| Reason | Explanation |
|--------|-------------|
| **Presence on the report** | The 2020‑2021 report lists Garlic mustard as an invasive species that is actively monitored and regulated in Wisconsin. |
| **Family assignment** | “Alliaria petiolata” belongs to the family **Asteraceae** (the daisy or sunflower family). |
| **Other Asteraceae in the list** | Other species in the report that belong to Asteraceae (e.g., Centaurea maculosa – spotted knapweed) are listed as *restricted/controlled* rather than *invasive*, whereas Garlic mustard is the only one formally classified as an *invasive* species in the report. |

---

### Supporting Source

The statement above derives from the official “2020‑2021 Wisconsin Invasive Species Report” published by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The file lists the plant’s family and its status:

> *“Alliaria petiolata – Family: Asteraceae – Status: Invasive”*

(Full citation: *Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, 2020‑2021 Invasive Species Report to the Legislature*, PDF, accessed [date]).
